newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem looks set to win Bosnia's presidential race.
newsitem.headline: Moslem looks set to win Bosnia's presidential race.

text.p: Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem, looked set to beat the leading Serb candidate to the top job in a new collective presidency after post-war elections, with a final result due on Tuesday.
A result had been expected on Monday but vote counting was slower than expected, election organisers said.
"It is now clear that the presidency count will not be established until tomorrow," Robert Frowick, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation (OSCE) mission in Bosnia, told reporters.

Late on Monday Izetbegovic had 170,107 votes compared to 121,391 for Momcilo Krajisnik, speaker of parliament in the current separatist Serb republic, with 38 of 109 municipalities reporting, said the OSCE.

The leader of Bosnia's main Moslem nationalist party also boasted an 82 percent to 15 percent lead over his opposition rival for the Moslem seat on the presidency, former prime minister Haris Silajdzic.
Krajisnik, a hard-line nationalist, was also far ahead of his Serb opposition rival for the presidency, with 78 percent of the vote compared to 19 percent for moderate Mladen Ivanic.
But while eastern Bosnia is a bastion of Krajisnik's Serb Democratic Party (SDS), around 70 percent of Bosnian Serbs live in the north where an opposition coalition is most popular.
Krajisnik's lead looked less assured in the northern town of Banja Luka, where he had 60 percent against 30 percent for Ivanic, with 70 percent of the votes counted.
In the race for the Croat seat on the presidency, nationalist Kresimir Zubak boasted a huge lead, 84 percent over 15 percent for centrist competitor Ivo Komsic.

Izetbegovic's party had feared Silajdzic might split the Moslem vote, allowing a Serb to emerge as head of the presidency. The senior member would act as Bosnia's head of state in foreign relations but the presidency will govern by consensus.
A team of international observers found no major irregularities, its director said in a preliminary report on Monday.

The generally upbeat post-mortem by chief observer Ed van Thijn, Coordinator for International Monitoring, made it likely the OSCE would certify the election outcome despite fraud allegations by parties and voters.

But van Thijn's report was larded with caveats. He said the OSCE should demand the dominant Bosnian Serb separatist party amend its charter to endorse a reunified Bosnia as a condition for validating the elections.

Van Thijn also urged the OSCE not to stage municipal elections later this year as planned unless a problem with rigged voter lists is rectified and freer movement is established across Bosnia's internal ethnic boundaries.
The Coordinator for International Monitoring in Saturday's elections, Van Thijn said almost 1,000 observers covered 65 percent of polling stations in 87 of 109 districts.
He stressed at a news briefing that his report was preliminary and should be "treated with caution".
Only 14,700 of a possible 150,000 refugees actually crossed communal lines to vote, many for fear of being assaulted. Van Thijn called this figure "very, very disappointing and unacceptable".
